description: Software Engineering students at Universidad Surcolombiana with a shared passion for software systems and space exploration. We learn continuously and enjoy turning programming logic into interactive tools and complex mission simulations.
summary:
Milky Mission is a cooperative mission-design simulator built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Players receive an objective, a fixed budget and one launch; they choose an orbit, a launch vehicle, a spacecraft bus, propulsion, power, communications and up to four scientific instruments, then select 3 of 6 mission requirements and simulate a full year of operations.

Six budgets — mass, power, cost, data, link and lifetime — recalculate on every change, so the consequence of a decision appears before launch. Warnings never block, except for physically impossible designs. The simulation is deterministic: the same design and seed always produce the same result, and a mission can be shared by URL.

NASA data drives the mechanics: DONKI supplies the real May 2024 storm timeline, POWER supplies irradiance and cloud cover for the optical-versus-radar trade-off, and every catalog value is tagged official, derived, estimate or game. The game runs offline, in English and Spanish, and ends with a report that explains the causal chain instead of a game-over screen.
details:
What it does and how it works. Milky Mission is a mission-design simulator for one to four players on a single screen. A team receives an objective, a fixed budget and one launch. It then chooses an orbit, a launch vehicle, a spacecraft bus, propulsion, a solar array and its area, a battery, a communications band, a ground network, on-board storage and up to four scientific instruments. Six budgets — mass, power, cost, data, link and mission lifetime — are recalculated synchronously on every change, so the consequence of a decision appears before launch. Players choose 3 of 6 mission requirements (5 in the second scenario), review the design against blocking errors and non-blocking warnings, accept the risks they are willing to carry, and then simulate 365 days of operations compressed into roughly 75 seconds. Every event is owned by a role and requires a decision with a real cost; a deterministic engine then produces a report with a score and a causal chain of what went wrong.

Benefits. The game makes engineering trade-offs visible and reversible. A team can redesign and re-fly in minutes, and the report explains causes rather than just results. No prior space knowledge is required: the brief, the tooltips and a "show the math" panel teach the minimum needed to decide.

Intended impact. Milky Mission is built for classrooms, science clubs and outreach events. It runs offline in a browser, works in English and Spanish, is keyboard accessible and never communicates status by colour alone. The second scenario, Andes Flood Watch, is grounded in a real local problem: Magdalena basin communities that get about twelve hours to evacuate when the river floods.

Tools and technology. React 19 and TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS v4, Zustand and Vitest, deployed as a static site on GitHub Pages through GitHub Actions. There is no backend and no account system. The simulation engine is pure TypeScript — no React, no DOM, no network — and computes mass from the rocket equation, orbit and eclipse geometry from Keplerian mechanics, power from irradiance, array area, packing, incidence and degradation, link performance from free-space path loss and C/N0, plus data delivery, cost and reliability. Every constant comes from a versioned catalog, never from the interface. The demo requires no hardware beyond a laptop.

How it is creative. The team never invents numbers: NASA data drives the mechanics. NASA DONKI supplies the real space-weather timeline for 1–15 May 2024, including the G5 storm with Kp 9.0 on 10–11 May. NASA POWER supplies monthly irradiance and cloud amount for the target regions, which makes the optical-versus-radar decision a real trade-off rather than a rule. NASA GIBS supplies the base imagery. Each value is tagged official, derived, estimate or game and audited in a provenance document, so a judge can trace any number to its source. Runs are seeded and deterministic: the same configuration always produces the same result, so a mission can be shared by URL and reproduced.

Factors considered. We balanced ambition against scope: we prioritised a complete, reliable end-to-end flow over a wider feature set, and deliberately left role tokens, difficulty levels and orbital mapping on the roadmap. We also considered classroom constraints (offline use, accessibility, bilingual copy, 1024 px screens) and scientific honesty (labelled confidence, monotonicity tests, balance bands: a reference mission scores 800–860 out of 1000 on 197 kg of 250 kg, 153 W against 99 W of load and $43.2M of a $50M budget; a naive design scores 500–650).

AI use. Code and documentation were drafted with AI coding agents — Gemini, Claude and GLM 5.3 — under mandatory human review, type checking and automated tests. Decorative illustrations are AI-generated and carry a visible watermark. No scientific data, formula or simulation result was generated by AI.
